english: He did not set this forth merely, but to demonstrate that it is God's will that all be called from Christ and that the apostles be so. He arranges himself as being known to the Corinthians, and he restrains the storm of those puffed up by words. He connects the badly occurred division to a single church, calling these from God; and he proposes [unity] in Jesus Christ, not in fear and dread. It must be observed how, in a few words, he often remembers Jesus Christ, teaching from the prefaces that it is fitting to be named from no other, but from our Lord Jesus Christ, and healing the wound caused by the divisions of different names through the continuous memory of Jesus Christ.

He says, 'Sanctified in Jesus Christ.' It is not man who has sanctified you, but God in Christ. For if he says one calls upon a man, he is named from this; but if Jesus Christ, he is named from Him whom he calls upon. And it is well with all those who call upon Him; for it is not you alone, but all who believe everywhere call upon Christ, and are named from Him, not from men. Therefore, do not alone welcome an impious novelty by introducing it. And he did not say 'with all those calling the name,' but 'to those calling upon Him,' showing God [who shows] the Son of God; for someone calls upon God in every place, both theirs and ours. If every place is one calling upon Jesus Christ, imitate the many, but do not alone do something strange apart from the others. Theirs and ours is joined to the Lord; instead of saying 'we the writers and you the enjoyers of the letters,' we have one Christ.

Concerning the restoration of the things set forth: for if grace is from our Lord Jesus Christ and not from men, he says, it is fitting to be named from Him. He persists in this same point. For if wealth is from Him, and if knowledge is from Him, why do you assign the name of teacher to one, the name of baptizer to another, the name of leader to another, and as if another were the provider? Therefore he says, 'leading before you'; for what do you have that you did not receive? And if indeed you received, why do you boast as if you had not received?

He says, 'in every word.' Since it is a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge, and many words of gifts, therefore he says: in every word and in all knowledge. Since there are also many distinctions of knowledge, [he says] in all knowledge. It was written to the Greeks, those who had not received the old and the new, and those possessing knowledge on both sides; just as the testimony of Christ was established in you. Regarding those begging for establishment, they are already incomplete. Thus he showed that they need correction, giving thanks for what they received, but being corrected for what they did not fulfill.

Faithful is God, through whom you were called. Since he said, 'God will establish,' he proceeded: Faithful is God—for God is true, being able to provide these things—through whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, not into a fellowship of man, but into the fellowship of His Son. Why, abandoning being named from the Son into whose fellowship you were called, are you being named from men? And again, that which lies through Him is upon the Father, not only upon the Son. And it is not a degradation to the Father, since through Him we are called into the fellowship of His Son; for it has not been written concerning the Romans that through Him and from Him and into Him are all things. Already God, because of that which is from Him which is greater than Himself, and because of that which is through Him which is lesser than himself—just as regarding the person lying upon the same, he does not make Himself both lesser and greater, so also he does not degrade the Son by that which is said through Him upon Him. english: He remembers being named by men, from the very beginning of the contests of the name of Jesus Christ, from which all ought to be called. He does not complain about what is currently being said regarding dogmas, nor does he complain to them about this, but rather about what we have said before and what he demonstrates hereafter.

He asks: Are you not heirs with Christ, with whom he shared you, the believers? For he did not say, 'Christ was shared,' but rather, 'did Christ not share with you?' The argument demonstrates this, for he says: Was not Paul crucified for us? The Christ died for the salvation of the world, but none of us. From this, he shows that some intended to be named after the one who was baptizing them. This good thing, which the Savior also commanded and which brings salvation, became a burden to me, he says, if you were intending to be called from me, the one baptizing.

How then are we to understand that Christ did not send me to baptize, but to evangelize? Since even one who is not an apostle baptizes, yet the dignity of the apostles was held by few, and without being evangelized and being baptized, one could not be baptized, he says; I was sent to evangelize, for this is the preceding thing, not to baptize. It is therefore left here, by implication, that 'I was not previously sent to baptize.' Thus also elsewhere when he says: Does God not care for the oxen? Not because he does not care; for even in the Law, Moses says concerning oxen, truly concerning those who serve the farmers. And David says: Lord, you will save men and cattle, just as God has multiplied your mercy. And Solomon says: The righteous man has pity on the souls of his cattle, how much more God? But what is it that he says? That previously God does not care for the oxen. And here, by ellipsis, it is as if he said, 'that Christ did not send me to baptize.'

Moving to another fault and coming to another correction, not having completely set aside the first, he has used the second as a prelude. For the first was that Christ did not send me to baptize, regarding the fact that each of you says: 'I am of Paul,' or 'I am of Apollos'; the second is the word not in wisdom, the beginning of another administration. Thus, evangelizing has been set as the end of the first matter and the beginning of the second, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.

The proclamation declares that the power of the cross is not displayed. Concerning the word of the cross, it does not speak of the mere utterance or the sound, but of the power; for while the work appears to be weak, the cause, when sought, is revealed to be a great mystery. To us who are being saved, it is the power of God. Since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and some desire to receive the word of God through Him, it must be observed that regarding the cross, the word speaks of the power of God.

For it is written: 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.' Even though the apostle is himself credible in his teaching—for he had Christ speaking within himself—he has also made use of the testimony of the Old Testament, producing a more certain certainty for the disciples. Having used the testimony, 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,' he proceeds as if upon what has already been agreed, saying: Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? The wisdom of the Greeks, and the scribe of the Jews.

He mentions two wisdoms: one is the harmony observed in the created things, and the other is the wisdom according to which men, being rational, become intelligent. Since, he says, through the understanding coming to us we did not know God, nor through the wisdom observed in the created things, God was pleased to save those believing through the foolishness of the proclamation. Great is what he says, which is not shown to those passing by simply; for the power of God and all-wisdom demonstrates itself in this way.

The magnitude and the beauty of the world, he says, being immeasurable and ungraspable, did not persuade you to know God; rather, leaving the Maker, you worshipped these things through which it was necessary to know their Maker. God, showing the excess of His own power—whom creation did not persuade but even struck—enlightened the world through the agreed-upon weakness of the cross.

For showing the absurdity of those who have been emboldened in rationality and think to adorn piety through eloquence, he says that we must not answer not only those seeking wisdom among the Greeks, but also those Jews who ask for signs—the signs of the Spirit, and the wisdom of the words of external education. If they do not even ask for the wonders of the Spirit, it would have been fitting to give them the things of external wisdom—for not...

γάρ–ἀλλ' αὐτὸς ἡμῖν σοφία γέγονεν εἰς θεογνωσίαν· οὐκ ἀνθρώπων σύνεσις

ἀσθενείᾳ καὶ ἐν φόβῳ καὶ ἐν τρόμῳ τὸ ἀσθενὲς ἐξ ὧν ἐδιωκόμην. ἐπεδεικνύμην τὸν
φόβον καὶ τὸν τρόμον τὸν περὶ ὑμῶν, πάντα ἤμην ταπεινός, ἵνα ὑμεῖς τούτῳ

english: They attempt to give, yet they ask in bad faith; the word is cast out entirely as one attacking the glory of the cross. But we preach Christ crucified and the following. It is evident that he says Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God according to the logic of the cross, as being superior; for the word of the cross is foolishness to those being destroyed, but to us being saved it is the power of God.

He demonstrates this more clearly after saying: to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, he brought Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. Who would dare say the Word God is the weakness of God, and the foolishness of God regarding the crucified Christ? God the Word is powerful as the Father, not a power as a part fulfilling the essence of the Father, and likewise wise; since that which the visible creation, or angels, or archangels, or patriarchs, or prophets, or the law through Moses, or the voices from the midst of the fire brought to the people—which could not forgive the choice of the ungrateful—this, the foolishness of the cross, prevailed.

Therefore, Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God, more incomparable to all the economy and more reliable than all creation. And this is the power of the one who dispensed and perfected, having saved men through nothing and having brought them into faith in him.

Since the Jews test the Spirit of God, but it is to be granted to the believers, it is also necessary to answer the Greeks who think they can order piety by rationality; then he teaches how the preaching seems to be foolishness. For they seek signs and wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, the power of God and the wisdom of God, and we promise salvation from the crucified one to those who believe.

It is not right to say the Word God is the weakness of God, but rather the cross of Christ; for the Word is powerful as the Father, not a power as a part fulfilling the essence of the Father. So also the Son is wise as the Father.

Not by angels, nor by law, nor by prophets, but because God forgives according to the choice of the ignorant, this thing which seems to be the foolishness of the cross has power. The crucified Christ is proclaimed as the power and wisdom of God, having been seen as stronger and more enduring, having saved those who believe. 1 Cor 1:26 The fleshly element was added, opposing the spirit, and the following things similarly give out according to the common. 1 Cor 1:29 So that no flesh may boast before Him; that is, so that the achievement of the preaching is not written upon the advantages of those at home. But he said 'flesh' and not 'soul', belittling human boastings. And why 'before Him' and not 'before men'? Because the boasting upon our own advantages was set in opposition to the boasting upon God. For what was necessary to write upon God, they were writing upon men. Therefore he said 'before Him'; for boasting occurring before Him, He who sees all, was impious. And that he said 'before Him' and not 'in the presence' is shown by this whole hypothesis; for those boast in words and in baptizing, and make the word about other things. 1 Cor 1:30

But of Him you are. All similarly say now that it has been said according to the being saved, not according to the logic of creation, as it is said elsewhere: those who were not born of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. If therefore [it is] of Him, how shall we boast in our own advantages? But [it is] in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom and sanctification and redemption; not the wisdom of men saved—for it was wandering—but He Himself has become wisdom for us unto the knowledge of God; not the understanding of men snatched away, but Jesus having been crucified. Not men redeemed, so that the boasting may be from the Savior, not from the saved. 1 Cor 2:3–4 I was always afraid lest you be puffed up by outward training, since I did not use the persuasive wisdom. And in weakness, he says, the weakness from persecutions—for this is his custom to say everywhere—in weakness and in fear and in trembling, the weakness of those from whom I was persecuted. I demonstrated the fear and the trembling concerning you, I was all humble, so that you might be taught by this and not be puffed up. Since he said: 'my word, so that the opposite might not glory'.

english: Presenting this, which is eloquence, he says: my preaching is not in persuasive words of wisdom, because wisdom is not of words but of divine knowledge, of spirit and power. Since indeed the Holy Spirit provides the word of wisdom and also performs wonders, he said: in the demonstration of spirit and power; for that which is called not yet a demonstration, but the wonder possesses the demonstration.

He shows that he did not preach relying on any human ability; for he was in weakness and fear and trembling and in such things, as if he were in persecutions and afflictions. Because merely speaking, he did not overcome those using wisdom and trusting themselves in the word, but performing powers he showed the strength of God, and from there the preaching was well brought forth: but in the demonstration of spirit and power, so that your faith might not be in human wisdom but in the power of God.

This is not in things considered estimable, but in those perfect according to piety. And in the perfect, he says, not indeed to the perfect ones, for one speaks to those happening to be present and often receives many contradictions, but he who introduces the saving word to the perfect and pious does not speak as if depositing and treasuring the words in their souls.

If it was hidden, it is clear that it was not of calculations to find it, but truly it was of God to reveal it. And the demonstration of not knowing, instead of saying: for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. And he calls the ones concerning Pilate and Herod 'rulers', but the incarnate God 'the Lord of glory'.

This use is not carried out for these rhetoricians in the old way, but signifying the same with other words; for Isaiah says: Lord, who believed our hearing? and to whom was the arm of the Lord revealed? and who will recount his origin? and Moses: the secret things belong to the Lord our God. But the secret of God, clearly, both eye and heart he has pierced. One must not think, however, that God strictly revealed the mystery to some and allowed others to perish in ignorance, but it is necessary to know and be convinced that by his foreknowing power he provided to each, measuring according to merit, that which is for their benefit; for he foresees each.

The depths of God have spoken his deepest things, which have surpassed us in administration. Through these things he shows that he searches, not as one ignorant but as one who knows. Since some say the Spirit is the Father and others the Son, one must speak regarding each separately. It is impossible to say the Father; for he says we received not the spirit of the world but the spirit from God, and no one of it is [the Father]; for if it were spoken about God, from whom is God? As for the Son, it is possible to suppose him, but to be that about whom the Word is not possible; for who would say the God-Word searches so that he might learn the things of God? If they said the Son is being taught, how would he not have known from the following that just as the spirit in him knew things as a human spirit, so also the Spirit of God. Apart from this, the Holy Spirit is shown throughout the whole field. It should be noted that the Holy Spirit he says is from God, but the unclean one he did not say is from the world but is of the world; for the Paraclete is not a part of God, whereas the devil, according to having come to be, is a part of the creation. But the Holy Spirit is from God.

Not so that he might show, as the spirit in us is better than us, so also in God the spirit is better than him, immediately saying: for what man knows the things of the man except the spirit in him? But what is in God? For the one in him shows a part being the completion of the whole man, but the one from him shows the cause. It should be noted that God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, but man and the spirit in him are not two persons but one man. Thus, showing the exact identity of the Father and the Spirit according to knowledge, he compared the knowledge of the spirit in us to the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit, so that it might be shown that in us, in the one and the same spirit, which is the soul and the mind, there is no discord of union; we know what we know, and so also in Father and Holy Spirit there is no discord of knowledge but identity. In order that we might know the things granted to us by God, the Spirit having given, the mind having grasped. And we speak. Again he shows another thing; not only says, not...

english: We find the things revealed to us within our own reasoning, but we also proclaim them; we do not decorate them with words, but rather we compare spiritual things to the spiritual, understanding those revelations by the power of the Spirit and proclaiming them in their proper order. We compare spiritual things to the spiritual because when the second revelation serves as an interpretation and a clarity of the former, those receiving the revelations compare the later things to the first, and finding the same, they receive a greater full-knowledge of the revealed truth.

God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, but man and the spirit in him are not two persons, but one man. He says this because just as there is no disagreement of knowledge within a man, so also the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit is one; for this reason, the Spirit would not have inquired as if he were ignorant. Furthermore, regarding the man, the Spirit in him spoke, but regarding the Holy Spirit, he did not say 'the one in God' but 'the one from God.' There is a great difference between the one in him and the one from God, for the one in him is the completion of the whole man, while the one from him shows the cause.

Precisely, the Holy Spirit from God spoke as a living and subsistent essence, but the unclean of the world spoke as its completion of essence; for the devil is a part of its creation according to how it came to be. However, we do not find the things revealed to us to be decorated by mere reasoning, but we compare spiritual things to the spiritual when the second revelation becomes an interpretation and a clarity of the first teaching, vision, or wonder. The later things are compared to the first and the same are found. We receive the greatest full-knowledge of the truth from this harmony. This is made manifest by those who compare opposites, and also by those who distinguish and separate; yet the former is better. 1 Cor 2:14-15 A natural man does not receive...

Concerning the Spirit. He calls the one who adheres to familiar reasonings 'psychic.' For it is foolishness to him. Such is the depth of the spiritual revelation that it appears as foolishness to the wise of this world; in this way, the revelation of God is uncontainable to them. For, demonstrating power through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he reproves the clever man, not by cleverness but by the strength of wonders. The spiritual ones do not overturn reasonings with reasonings, but receiving the mind from God and the revelation from there, they discourse, so that the one opposing does not refute reasonings, but opposes the knowledge of God. Because of this he says: for who has known the mind of the Lord, who will instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ, which is the knowledge.

He calls 'psychic' the one adhering to familiar reasonings, or the one sick with the reasonings of the soul and not being strong concerning the knowledge of the truth, just as he calls 'fleshly' the one sick concerning fleshly desires and a slave to pleasures. Thus, the psychic is not able to be receptive to the truth, but has so corrupted the soul as to regard the economy of God and the grace as foolishness. And, being unable to know that he is being examined spiritually, the psychic man, seeking clever reasonings, regards the cross as foolish and, having lost faith, is pushed away from the preaching; and not rejecting the wonders of the Spirit, he is no longer able even to perceive that he is being refuted by the power and wonder of the Spirit against the truth; for 'to examine' reveals the precise and is to refute thoroughly. But the spiritual man, who has come to possess the Spirit through whom he demonstrates signs, refutes all those who refute poorly, while he himself is refuted by nothing. Furthermore, believing the word, he sets forth things from the old and says (1 Cor 2:16): 'He will instruct.' We have the mind.

english: Of Christ our God. If men do not grasp the mind of God to know, how much less will they grasp the mind of us who possess the mind and wisdom of God. 1 Cor 3:1–3 Those unfaithful follow miracles rather; therefore I spoke a word to you, not indeed the perfect wisdom which is hidden, the administration concerning the passion which only perfect believers receive.

He still calls the teaching concerning ethics and the believing through signs 'milk' in a figurative sense, but the proclamation of the divine dogmas is 'meat'. Light commands can be milk, such as honoring father and mother, and not committing adultery, and the like, and 'come here, follow me'. Then, having said, 'You are fleshly, and walk according to man', he says that you honor things in man and do not seek the things of God. 1 Cor 3:5 Instead of being equal according to the ministry. 1 Cor 3:6–10

The things spoken to him were as if concerning agriculture, and the others as if concerning building. He himself said he has planted and has given the beginning and has laid the foundation of God. He exhorts those building after him at the foundation, so that they do not work the building in vain. And he calls the foundation the faith and the proclamation. 1 Cor 3:11–15

Christ is not called the foundation of the creation, as the Arians falsely contend, but of the faith; for Christ was proclaimed, and every building happens upon him as the foundation. While some are teaching one faith and proclaiming the evangelical life, for us it is to make ourselves either precious stones or wood or grass or a reed. When therefore he says, 'Let each one let him see how he builds', he means not according to life, but according to what? For no one is able to lay a foundation other than the one lying there.

The one teaching proclaims Christ and gives his commands; therefore it is to be separated either by gold because of purity, or by grass because of weakness. If therefore he commands that each one let him see, it is toward those wishing to be named among those baptizing or teaching. If anyone's work remains which he built up, you see that the builder builds well; but that does not remain according to a change of human choice at times. If anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, and so as through fire. It is surpassing.

For it is to be read this way: if anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, and it will be as through fire; so that he will be burned and suffer loss as through fire, yet he himself will be saved, for the more grievous deviation did not occur through him. It has been said by the transcendent so that it might be thus: if anyone's work remains, he will receive a reward, but he himself will be saved. If anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss and be burned as through fire. How then will he be saved if the work he built is burned? Thus, as he is judged as through fire, did he fail to leave behind those coming for correction or the reminding of those sinning, according to Ezekiel?

Again, he turns to those who trust in their own wisdom. For while he calls the believers the temple of God, he also says that one destroys the temple of God. He will declare the following to those who trust in words. If anyone thinks to be wise in this present age, let him become a fool. For why then does the one trusting in external wisdom destroy the temple? If you are a temple of God, you owe it to have one who teaches and reveals; but if, having left the Inhabitant, you have used your own understanding, you no longer make a temple, but you destroy it.

If anyone thinks to be wise among you, it is those being harmed and deceived by external education, for he commanded, having said among you. Regarding those who have been catechized and have received the word of knowledge within themselves, and have not strayed from the teaching, he calls them temples of the Holy Spirit and immovable houses of the indwelling Spirit. But those who have done something worthy of the energy of the Spirit, he calls these spiritual, just as we call those who have made a display of art and rhetoric 'rhetorical' and 'technical.'

Therefore, those receiving a different teaching from external wisdom, these have destroyed their own reasoning, corrupting the faith, which is the temple of the Spirit. Consequently, God threatens that these will be destroyed, because having abandoned the indwelling Teacher, they wandered regarding external wisdom, which is sufficient to provide a supply of deception. Through this, by which he forbids the wisdom of this world from being sufficient for deception, he commanded those being struck by reproof. Commanding that external wisdom not be received, he teaches not to boast upon wise men.

english: For this boasting is cheap, where everything belongs to you: the apostles—for they were sent for the sake of those being helped—the world, which has become yours for enjoyment, your life, as those being saved, and death; for if the things of death were not fearsome, the things of the coming life would not have been prepared. For by the same logic, the present and the future are spoken of; for those who despise the present things think they attain the future things.

Therefore all these things said of you, that you yourselves have become Christ's, and that those belonging to Christ please God, are all through you. How and in what way? That you yourselves have become Christ's, and in order to show that those belonging to Christ please God, he added: Christ is God's.

It is sufficient for us to be esteemed as servants of Christ, though from us some are named slanderers. You see us as servants of God, but what servant is faithful? Do not seek it—for this is in danger among you—and it is not worthy for teachers to be judged by students. Why does he say these things? Because he realized that some of the teachers were being punished by them as unworthy, while the worthy were being reviled, whence he foresaw schisms coming among them. Therefore he more vehemently accuses, hurrying to restrain the passion.

So that he might not seem to say these things as if being contemptuously despised, he says this only once: do not think that I send these things on my own behalf; for I do not conduct myself in such a way that I be interrogated by you; for I consider this unworthy toward you and toward every man. He calls man a human day, signifying the temporary and ephemeral nature of human life.

Then, because it seems great to say 'I have said nothing against myself,' he added 'but I have not been acquitted by this'; for one who has stumbled through ignorance is not to be struck in the conscience. Furthermore, not failing to do something justifies, but doing rightly perfects virtue. And it is likely that he said this with moderation: therefore do not judge me greater or less than you, but wait for the Judge. This serves the whole purpose of making sober those who wish to be named this or that, or not to be named this or that; for in judging these things, it is the one both worthy and unworthy.

Therefore, do not think highly of yourselves, but wait for the Judge; for while a corrupted character may deceive you, the one who illuminates the secrets of darkness will not let anything hidden escape him. He said these things because much happened among them through deception and they were honored unworthily. Those being honored were not entirely good, but their virtue reached only to the appearance, while those who were naturally good were being overlooked; for he would not have said these things.

He presents himself and Apollos, silencing the faces of those demanding honor and being called disciples by them, so that you might take from us a pattern and a following to approach teachers moderately. And do not think beyond what is written concerning us, but consider us servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God, and do not dishonor the former, but honor the latter. He clarified their opinion more clearly in these things; for he who is named by that [other] and yet circumscribes that [other], is puffed up by the former but has the character of the latter.

You, who desire to be called by this one or to leave that one, who distinguishes? Do you not wait for the Judge? You, the obedient one, wait for the Judge, yet you subject the teacher to your own judgment? Who distinguishes you, the common people, regarding those things about which you think or act, that you dare to distinguish others and these [people] teachers? Is it not the Lord? If then you, the disciple, wait for the Lord as Judge, how do you subject the teacher to your judgment, calling the one worthy and the other unworthy? Why do you think you have an advantage which you do not have or have not received? But he speaks of the surpassing understanding through which it is possible both to judge and to test teachers. Even if you received understanding from God, it is necessary to offer glory to God who gave it, not to think greatly of yourself and to be puffed up as if an advantage were being presented to you as your own possession.

It is not that they had such things, but they show that they were spreading falsehoods about themselves, thinking they were filled with all knowledge as a remainder to judge even teachers. Already the gifts have become a reality for you, and not always a thing to be desired. That which is apart from us shows that you have already reached the state of reigning without us, and indeed it is a loss through the midst.

english: Having shown his disposition concerning them, he says that in order that we also might reign with you, it is evident that they consider their own achievements as their own good. He does not read 'you have reigned and become rich' merely as a question, so that what was spoken might be in character for those who have already been disciplined.

For as I see, if you have become rich and have reigned without us, we have become the very last and most abominable, enduring all things. To men, he says, as they see our evils, but to angels, as they marvel at our standings. The same applies to these things. Those teaching you in contempt and in poverty, as being considered fools by the world, yet you, the taught ones, desire to be in the wealth and honors of Christ. He says these things to show that in spiritual gifts there is no student superior to the teacher.

We endure all things through Christ, and until now we humble ourselves. And how is it possible for you, living in the flesh, to be preferred by God over those who are laboring, being persecuted, being reviled, and being struck? He instructs through all these things how the Christian must be and how he must humble himself. Instead of the scraps, as if having been taken as refuse and filth from a house having been cleaned, we have become being despised by all, and we are the refuse of all, having set ourselves before all men through Christ. The 'wiping' is said to be the cloth which wipes the sweat of the laborer and removes the sickness lying upon him. Having strongly cleansed through the first things, he exhorts through these to win the power of salvation through the astringents and the sweet things.

By calling himself father, and those others pedagogues from whom they were called, he shows that he has a more genuine disposition toward them than the others, and that as being admonished by a father, they ought not to be indignant. In not being arrogant toward anyone and in becoming imitators of me, and in not being called by anyone but by Christ. See that those things said to him—we the weak, you the strong, and all the other things—were said toward the purpose of some being puffed up.

I will come to you quickly, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the words of those naturally gifted, but the power. Through this power he says he also reproves strongly, and he himself testifies to the suitability for restoration by threatening his own presence. For as if they were appearing humbled, he promises his presence, being corrected by the word before the presence. But he added 'if the Lord wills'; because of indignation he was driven to say that he would come, but because of reverence he was reminded to add the most beautiful addition, 'if the Lord wills'. And here he reveals what he previously had veiled so as not to reprove too harshly. For the kingdom of God is not in word, as is evident to the well-trained; for the apostles did not teach and preach without word. It is also evident from these things that what was said regarding some being naturally gifted was that we are weak and you are strong.

He promises his presence so that, if we arrive, we may correct ourselves. Therefore, because of indignation he was compelled to say 'I will come', but because of reverence he added 'if the Lord wills'. It became clearer from these things also that he is indignant toward those boasting in the wisdom of this world; for he does not intend to reproach the common man with words. He proclaimed this to all of them.

Since the restoration is twofold—one way through exhortation to the persuadable, and another way through force and necessity to the hard-hearted—he has acted philanthropically toward this faction of them, so that, repenting, they might correct themselves. He spoke of a rod, the necessary power of the Spirit, which Paul used according to Elymas and against Paul himself. It was not because he had the manner of speaking of a woman, but because he was respectable; and they did not grieve because he had a father's woman, but they were indignant because he was well-trained. For their grief either separated the fornicator from remaining, or it cut off the impropriety of the matter and brought him back. He did not simply work but had worked; for he did not fall having been seized, but used the work of evil. And he says to be present in spirit, agreeing and judging with him—but the spirit is...

english: He says 'gift'—having been gathered together with the power of Christ. Those who were puffed up because of the one who committed fornication were part of the whole, but he calls all to be gathered together for the condemnation of the fornication. They said it was the spirit, not the soul, but the gift.

He does not allow one to be moved by glory without reason, and he brings forward the cause of the wrath, because not only fornication, but such things are heard among you as are not even among the Gentiles. And think greatly that you have been adorned with the wisdom of the world. It is necessary to mourn over him because he has not even dared to make fornication common to others. For this mourning either separated the fornicator, who remained in fornication, or it separated the impropriety itself and brought the man back, so that the spirit might be saved.

He did not say 'not having worked' but 'having worked it out,' even so that by this it might appear that, having used much endurance, he worked out the evil, and was not snatched away by sin, so that he might have a defense. Indeed, the apostle alone was sufficient to condemn him, but he wants the Corinthians to be in agreement with him, so that he might thus build up, being separated from the fellowship of the lawless, especially those nurtured in instruction.

He does not do this as one subjecting him to the authority of Satan—for if he were inflating this by doing so, he would be puffing up Satan—but because we have become accustomed to assigning all the difficult things of life to Satan, such as diseases, sorrows, griefs, and other trials, just as the apostle himself says: 'A thorn of Satan was given to me, so that he might lash me.' In this very way, he now commands him to hand him over to Satan, which is to say, to the difficulties of life.

He delivers him to the harms of life; for this is for the destruction of the flesh, not for the destruction of the soul, so that, being awakened by the things happening to the body, he might repent and the spirit within him, which is the gift, might be saved. For he does not speak here of the soul as being of the flesh, but...

Standing, with the soul alone being saved. Regarding 1 Corinthians 5:6, you see that they were boasting over him, not paying attention to the impropriety of the fall, but being puffed up by his conceit. For they were boasting over him, not paying attention to his fall but being puffed up by his upbringing. He commands him to be expelled, so that the others, joining with him in sinning, might not be incited shamelessly.

In 1 Corinthians 5:7, he calls sin an old leaven, with which the old man was leavened together. He moves the type to the truth; for the unleavened things among the Jews, not having been leavened with old leaven, represent the new men, not having been leavened with the sins of the old man. The lamb being sacrificed among the Jews revealed the passion and the cross as a mystery of the economy. And he says the following: since the leaven is more complex, but the unleavened is simpler.

In 1 Corinthians 5:8, he admonished in this way, as if he were saying: not in an evil and bad life, but in a life not having mixture with that old leaven; for this is in unleavened bread, sincerity and truth. Regarding 1 Corinthians 5:9–10, he wrote not in another letter, but in this one. Because of this, he does not forbid those outside from eating, since if he were turning away all such people, the preaching would be hindered; for all such people, as it is said, are among the Gentiles whom it happened to benefit from the fellowship of those having believed. He therefore shows to strike those at home who sin, and to exhort those who have been rebuked.

In 1 Corinthians 5:9, 13, 'What I wrote is not of another letter but of this,' for he says: 'But now I have written to you.' And 'to purge the evil one from among yourselves' is a voice of Moses, which Paul repeats. He remembers a saying in the old text, showing that not only are they benefited as if being freed from some plague, but such a thing is not a novelty; rather, it also seemed good to the Lawgiver to cut off such people. english: A person becomes a judge of their own household, not of others. But God is the judge of all, since He is the master of all.

He reproaches them because the holy ones, who are able to judge, were judging against them by the unbelievers. Having said, 'You judge those within, but God judges those without,' He now subjects the whole world to the judgment of the holy ones. For in this life, they examine the lives of the faithful for their restoration, but for the judgment of the world, they entrust it to God, not for the restoration of the sinful ways, but for their exposure and condemnation. The twelve apostles judge the twelve tribes as Jews from among Jews, from whom they believed the prophets, even if they were unbelieving and for this reason turned away from Christ. The other holy ones, that is, the Gentiles, condemn those who did not turn from idols but believed in the true God. Thus there is no disagreement between the evangelist and the apostle, for Christ spoke in both; for it is written: a Queen of the South will rise and condemn this generation, and men of Nineveh will arise and condemn you.

Did He not say, 'And the world is judged by you'? Now He does not speak of angels according to nature, but of the ministers, the priests, the teachers of the people, who are likely to be judged by the holy ones as those handing down things concerning Christ. For having said, 'Is it not about practical matters?', He showed that He did not speak concerning natural angels, but concerning those having an angelic rank and performing spiritual deeds. If He spoke strictly of angels, it would be clear He meant those who have turned away and fallen from God. Yet priests were called angels according to Malachi, saying: 'The lips of a priest shall preserve knowledge, and they shall seek law from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord of powers.' Therefore, we judge these priests who led the people astray, just as those who began heresies and turned away from the teaching of Christ.

The least of the church is more contentious than the unbeliever. However, it seems the apostle leaves this out, which is clear: that the greater matters must be guarded by the perfect. You seem defeated by the devil, not only in judging the unbelievers, but also...

He holds judgments with one another. Regarding the single energy of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he spoke to the righteous, teaching the oneness of essence. He does not speak concerning a person, but concerning a matter from the subordinate; for the word is about these things: foods for the stomach, and the stomach for the foods, but God will abolish both this and that.

He does not speak concerning a person, but concerning an absurd matter and a passion. Yet, speaking about himself, he exhorts the others to self-control. Knowing that the stomach is the cause of their greed—for many dare all things because of the pleasures of the stomach—he teaches that it is unseemly to serve the stomach. We know that foods are for the stomach. It has been set apart from these things, yet nonetheless God will abolish these temporary things; for after the resurrection, when immortality is given, the need for surplus foods is lacking. Why then do you strive for temporary things, from which sexualities and pleasures are absurd?

For it is clear that foods and eating are temporary. But the body has been set apart not for sexual immorality but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body; and the body would not be temporary, but it will be raised into incorruption according to the type of Christ. He says body and members of Christ, the body of those having believed and having been baptized.

Therefore, if anyone sins in feeding or in defiling the body, he fulfills the need for it and for the honor of the body; but the one clinging to a prostitute, making one body with her, insults and dishonors his own body. The clothes and the world are outside of the body; therefore, the one doing these things outside of the body sins, whether one is slandering or lying to others, causing loss and seizing, or someone commits adultery with another woman; but the one committing sexual immorality insults himself, passing into the harm from the deed. Whatever then a man sins, he indeed sinned, but not into his own body, nor did he dishonor his own flesh like the one committing sexual immorality.

And indeed, the one who stains the hand with blood, a murderer, sins into his own body, and the slanderer [stains] the tongue as if with blood through slanders; but the one committing sexual immorality, he says, baptizes his whole self into...

γὰρ λοίδορος ἢ ἅρπαξ ἢ πλεονέκτης εἰς ἄνθρωπον ἐπλημμέλησεν ὃν ἐλοιδόρησεν ἢ

μόνον ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσέβειαν ἂν ἐγκληθήσεται ὡς τὰ μέλη τοῦ Χριστοῦ ποιῶν πόρνης
μέλη, καὶ εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ὡς εἰς ναὸν ὑβρίζων Χριστοῦ. διὸ καὶ ἐπάγει· ἢ οὐκ

ἀνεύθυνα–πάντα γὰρ ἔκπτωσιν ἔχει τῆς βασιλείας–ἀλλ' ὅτι πρὸς τὸ προκείμενον
ἐσπούδασε χαλεπωτέραν ἀποφῆναι τὴν πορνείαν ἁπάντων, πρόρριζον τὸ πάθος

english: Fornication is filth. Paul, therefore, by many inferences, grasped the idea that other sins exist outside the body. Others say that this sin has the explicit meaning of the mind, because he who fornicates sins against his own body; that is, against the constitution of his own body and against the human construction itself, and against the principles of our generation, as if he were saying: stop, thus through unlawful mixture you insult the workshop of nature from which even your own body has been defiled.

Others, out of zeal for Paul, say it is better to demonstrate the sin of fornication. Having said earlier, 'Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ,' and having shown from this that he who fornicates fails regarding the members of Christ, he thus shows that every sin follows in this way: for the slanderer, the robber, or the covetous man has sinned against a man whom he slandered or wronged, but he who has fornicated against his own body sins, which is a member of Christ. For as soon as one is completed into the body of Christ through the adoption of the Spirit, he would be accused not only of fornication but also of impiety, as making the members of Christ the members of a prostitute, and insulting his own body as if it were the temple of Christ.

Therefore he also proceeds: 'Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit in you, of whom you have from God?' For the sin of fornication regarding the body is as if you sin against the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit flees. This is not because the other sins lack direction—for all have a fall from the kingdom—but because in view of what lies ahead, he strove to make the fornication of all appear more severe, desiring to uproot the passion by cutting it off at the root, as sinning more impiously among the Corinthians; for entirely, he says, fornication is heard among you and the following. He who fornicates is also responsible for impiety, for having insulted his own body, he defiled the temple of the Holy Spirit.

And he says these things because some were fornicating contemptuously, regarding fornication as a small slip or no slip at all, not even remembering Moses in his Decalogue. But the salvation blood of Christ, which he gave as a ransom for us, is honor. Glorify therefore God not only in the gift but also in...

Regarding the body, so that both nature and choice and gift may glorify God. Indeed, glorify God in your body and in your spirit. Do this not only in the gift but also in the body, so that both nature and choice and grace may glorify the Benefactor through harmony. Others, however, the spirit has taken the soul.

These things he wrote to the lot, for from him also it was written to the apostle. He forbade fornication as lawless, but he permitted the fellowship of marriage as godly and free from fornication, and he commended self-control as more perfect. He teaches that those joined in marriage master one another rather than themselves. It is a good debt to those living together, when they know to pay to one another as a debt according to this same harmony. The apostle used such an economical descent so as to cut off fornication, the worst disease, by teaching that those joined in marriage master one another rather than themselves.

Since he said they are to be slaves to one another, he follows this by saying that they ought not to deprive one another, unless it be according to godly harmony, so that they may not become causes of the fornication of others, nor destroy the mastery over one another by dividing against the wills of others. Sympathizing with the nature of the body, I say how you ought to come together again, since I do not altogether say this while excluding your self-control; for I wish all to be in self-control just as I am.

To the widows and to the unmarried men who have not practiced virginity, he advises practicing self-control; but if they were overcome by the flesh, let them marry, showing that self-control is great. However, he permits marriage as a good bond. Regarding the woman not separating from her husband, he was not speaking of those separating and returning to Christ. Or let her be reconciled to her husband, or let her remain unmarried, as is shown concerning those dividing because of some strife. Above, concerning separation, he spoke of that through self-control; here, of that happening through contention. Then he said: Not I, but the Lord; for there is something which the apostle says from himself, but not all things the Lord says through himself. He says, however, that I command you now, what the Lord commanded in the Gospels concerning the married, having said what God...

english: A man has joined [them], let not one separate. In accordance with these things, if even if [one] is separated, let him remain unmarried, according to what was said to them by the Lord: if anyone marries one who is [already] married, he commits adultery, and that woman also if she is married to another.

He does not speak as one opposing the law, saying, 'I, not the Lord,' but rather that for some the Lord spoke by himself, while for others it is now first said by the apostle concerning the separation of the unbeliever, teaching that unbelief does not prevail over faith, but the faith of the one who is joined sanctifies even the unbeliever. He does not say that the unbeliever is to take [a spouse], but to endure the unbeliever. The children are holy, not defiled or by the unbelief, for the faith of the parents overcomes them more than the unbelief.

To one God has distributed the salvation, and to another to be saved, assigning to each his own portion. He does not say that each is to have an unbeliever as God has distributed, but to endure the unbeliever. Circumcision is not good for its own sake, but because it is a commandment of God, and uncircumcision is a creation of God, not a reward for the uncircumcised.

He says these things concerning the slave: do not strive for temporary freedom, but even if you are able, rather use the slavery; for the reward is greater when, being occupied with the slavery of men, one does not neglect to please God. Let each one remain in that state in which he was called: the slave in his slavery not complaining, and the free man not being arrogant, for there is no difference before God. The faithful slave has nothing less than this free man; for before God, a slave is seen as a free man and by Him is freed. This is shown by the fact that the one released from the master is the master's freedman, and that he is freed from the master; and the one called free into the faith will have nothing more than the slave, but similarly to him he is a slave of Christ.

Instead of living unworthily and without freedom through needs while healing people, you leave the true Master, in whose blood you were purchased. Grace does not know the difference between slavery and lordship. Therefore do not flee the slavery as if unworthy of faith; for you have nothing less than those in faith because of this. And if it is possible for you to attain freedom, let it be more of a care to you so that...

If you are able to use more, do so by exercising care within the freedom from evil. He demonstrates that neither does the free person in Christ possess more because of this, nor is the slave diminished; rather, it is for this reason that the situation is reversed. For the one called a slave in the Lord is a free person from the master, and likewise, the free person called a slave is Christ's. Regarding the test of the Christ speaking in me, he says: 'Do I not have a command?' For who would accept it if he were saying what the Lord had not commanded him? But it is clear that he is not saying this to teach a command concerning virginity, but rather that he did not receive from God the command for you to be virgins, but rather to give an opinion and to advise that virginity is good and useful.

Therefore, as one who advises, I think he calls it good and places the choice of embracing it upon those who hear. Since the matter is pleasing to God, just as the Lord said that certain people made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom, he calls virginity a form of eunuchism because it is inactive. He says, therefore, that he does not have a command, but he persisted in his opinion, saying, 'Let him who is able bear it.' After calling himself faithful, he shows that he speaks faithful things worthy of a command. I think that he says virginity is good not out of hesitation, but to secure that it is not regarded as a command.

He showed that he introduces virginity not as a condemnation of marriage, but that through concern for holy things, virginity is introduced, as marriage fills the flesh with pains and labors. He showed that he introduces virginity not as a condemnation of marriage, but as a release for those caring for worldly affairs. Having said, 'I have concern for you,' he introduces virginity through concern for the holy, not as a condemnation of marriage. He gives another reason for which he prefers virginity, showing everywhere that he prefers holiness over the condemnation of marriage; for the world is at its end, and it is necessary to know that what we have, we do not have—for we are leaving these things—so that those who have may be as those who do not have. If it is good for those who have to act as those who do not have, how much more for the virgin not even to approach marriage? And those using this world as if not using it cast out the immeasurable enjoyment through this, but the need.

english: It leaves behind. For the producing of the form of this world demonstrates that it is not the world itself that passes away, but rather the form of the present life is being transformed, corruption into incorruption: the cities, the walls, the laws, the agriculture, and the crafts. For these are like a certain form superimposed upon this life which undergoes change. Through this, the brevity of human life is made manifest, so that men might come to repentance, having wasted their lives and having despised the end of temporary things. And if it is good for those who possess marriage to have it as those who do not possess it, how much better is virginity? Let neither the sorrows of this life cast you down, nor let the things that seem like joys over-exult you; for all things here are temporary and do not stand. Form and a certain shape—like the cities, laws, agriculture, crafts, and trades of the world, of which there is much need—being changed from corruption into incorruption, shows therefore that not the world passes away, but the present form of the world.

He showed through this why he said, 'But I desire for you,' so that you might not empty your cares in things that do not remain. The following demonstrates this even more clearly. He provided the reason for which virginity is preferred to marriage; not because of the bed or the abstaining from the bed, but because the mind, which is filled with the cares of marriage, is occupied in godliness. I want you to be without anxiety, so that you might not empty your cares by being distracted by the needs of life that do not remain. Therefore also virginity is preferred to marriage, not because of the abstaining from the bed, but because it occupies the mind in piety.

Some suppose that he says he is acting unseemly regarding himself, whereas if anyone thinks he acts unseemly regarding his own virginity, it is not so. The following demonstrates this: for he says, 'So that he who divorces does well, and he who does not divorce does better.' But no one divorces himself, but is given by another.

It is better for this blessed one to remain in this state, for the one is for bodily rest, but the other is for a more perfect piety. This is stated for comparison: it is indeed blessed if she is married and has the protection of a man, but more blessed if, casting aside marriage, she is not married but occupies herself with God.

Since the Corinthians were eating things sacrificed to idols, saying that to us it is nothing to eat things sacrificed to idols—for we sanctify them by the name of Christ and eat—he shows that they alone will not be equal to the wise in knowing this, and says: we know that we all have knowledge. Thus, what you know, I know; but what you suffer, I do not suffer. This, that you know and I know, is not what must be considered; but what I know, that it is necessary not to eat because of the weak, this you do not know, but I know. Why then are you puffed up by a knowledge that does not possess as much as my knowledge? He proceeds: if anyone thinks he knows something among you, he has not yet known as it is necessary to know. Immediately, what I know, you do not yet know. But if anyone loves God, he has been known by Him. We, as far as we have become accustomed as humans to know, do not yet know anything. And what is the blessed thing? To love God and to be known by Him, not because He ignores those not loving, but because He makes the lovers His own; for knowledge is taken even unto making one's own, just as ignorance is unto making one a stranger, such as that which was said by the Lord, 'You went away, I never knew you.'

Since the Corinthians were saying: there is no idol, therefore we do not consider the sacrificial things, eating in the name of Christ rather than being harmed, he shows that not they alone as wise will be equal to this, but also others, that there is nothing sacred; so that what one knows, one knows, but what one suffers, one does not suffer. Such knowledge indeed puffs up and harms, if you know your own things, not to mention the other, that love builds up, for it is necessary for you because of love.

english: Lest a weak brother eat in an idol, so that he himself might be struck. He who thinks he knows something knows nothing; for he did not know that others were being harmed by this knowledge. Even if we think we know something, we do not yet know anything. But the blessed thing is to love God and to be known by him, which is to belong to him; for no one is truly ignorant, but the ungodly are said to be ignorant.

Having forewarned that there is no God but one, so that the Son might not be cast out from divinity, the Father brought him forth; for truly there is no other Father but one. Likewise, there is no other Son who is God but one. If one Lord is said of the Son, the Father is not lesser, which makes it clear that it is also as one God said of the Father. Neither is the God less, nor the Son. What is from him declares not the essence—for the creatures are not from the essence of God—but it declares that from which the will of the Father is shown.

Then, having said 'we in him' as well, he gives us to perceive what is lacking in the word: that 'but one God in us,' and we hope in him. Again, the word lacks 'and we through him'—for it lacks 'that we are called' or 'that we shall be saved'—for he does not say that through him we came to be, having said that all things encompassed him and us; but he says all things that came to be, while we [speak of] the things being dispensed and being saved. That which is made right for you is nothing, but that which harms the weaker is great.

What kind [of knowledge]? That one is God and there is no idol in the world. He who does not have this knowledge, that one is God and there is no idol in the world, thinking he eats something offered to idols, is struck. And your own knowledge harms the weak; for many even of those who have believed have not yet understood that there is no food offered to idols, and these are harmed by the believing one who eats. And that which is made right from eating is not great, but that which harms the weaker is heavy.

I do not say that I shall not eat food offered to idols, but not even meat, if on this account the brother is stumbled, for he did not have authority in those things, such as to write among them, to endure any weight. He prepares this through many things, and first he remembers his own command, to show the reasons why he took [meat] lawfully, and if he had wished to take it, just as with the others from whom they took. I also, he says, from...

I am an envoy and I possess my own authority, and I am not under anyone who forces me or prevents me from taking it; for even if the other apostles possess more than I regarding becoming with Christ, I am not deprived of this. Regarding those asking me if I am an apostle, this is my defense, which is your own seal and teaching. Do I not ordain as an apostle? Do I not legislate for the churches? Am I not taught by others? I indeed have authority, but I do not use it excessively, so that I might not cause some little-believers to stumble.

This is the confirmation and the proof. It shows that it has been legislated for those who serve, whether by altars or by the gospel, to live from these things. By mentioning a wife and adding a sister, he showed what is fitting, modest, and pure for one living in common, whether she was a wife or not, clearly showing that women also lived in common with Peter and others, desiring their teaching. He does not slander these things—may it never be—but shows the excess of his own precision regarding his life, warning the Corinthians not to live without caution, so that they might not become a stumbling block to others.

Was it forbidden to do these things only to us, which are also done to others? He placed Barnabas as a fellow-worker, so that he might not seem to magnify himself as the only one succeeding. I do not speak my own words; does not the law also say these things? I did not write this so that I might gain something from you, may it never be. It is nothing great, if an idol-sacrificed morsel is taken for the sake of your brother; for I also enslaved myself to things to which I am not subject, in order to benefit many.

He says Jews are those who are by nature of the Israelite race, but under law are those who are not of their race, namely those using the law of the Jews and having become proselytes. He says the Greeks are lawless, those who are not under the law of Moses. He did not say to the Greeks, 'I became a Greek,' because he could not endure pretending to be Hellenism. Therefore, he calls lawless those who turned from the Gentiles. I thought the Greeks were not under law and I held the opinion, in order to save them from the Jewish things. Thus he was giving to all the primary principle of bringing himself along, so that being caught with them, he might win a few to himself.

μὴ κεχρῆσθαι νόμῳ, ἐμιμησάμην αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκονομίαν, ὅπερ ἐκεῖνο βούλεται

χρῆσθαι νόμῳ, ἐμιμησάμην αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκονομίαν· ὅπερ γὰρ ἐκεῖνο εἶπεν, τοῦτο

καὶ ἀπέγνωσαν ἑαυτῶν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἰς τὸ δυσκατόρθωτον ἀποβλέποντες–ἀλλὰ
δηλονότι ἡ εἰκὼν πρὸς τὰ εἰρημένα αὐτῷ ἔθνη εἴληπται. πάντες, φησίν, ὡς ἐν
σταδίῳ τῷ βίῳ τούτῳ ἀγωνίζονται,Ἰουδαῖοι μὲν κατὰ νόμον,Ἕλληνες δὲ κατὰ
πλάνην, εἷς δέ ἐστιν ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας λόγος, ὁ νικῶν καὶ λαμβάνων τὸ βραβεῖον. διὸ
τρέχετε ἵνα μὴ σὺν τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀπολειφθῆτε. 1 Kor 9,25 Τί μέγα, φησίν, ἐὰν
ἐγκρατεύσησθε σαρκὶ διὰ τὸν ἀδελφόν; πάντα δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν ἀγωνιζόμενον,
ἀπὸ θυμοῦ, ἀπὸ δόξης καὶ ἀπὸ πάντων τῶν λοιπῶν· ἐκεῖνοι μὲν οὖν ἵνα φθαρτὸν
στέφανον λάβωσιν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἄφθαρτον. Τοῦτο οὐχ ἁπλῶς εἶπεν, ἀλλὰ διορθούμενος
τοὺς ἕνεκεν τοῦ 258 γαστρίζεσθαι φιλοσοφεῖν προσποιουμένους, ὅτι τὸ εἰδωλόθυτον
οὐκ ἔστιν εἰδωλόθυτον. 257,ξολ2 Οὐχ ἁπλῶς τοῦτο εἶπεν ἀλλὰ διορθούμενος τοὺς
ἕνεκεν τοῦ 258,ξολ2 γαστρίζεσθαι ἀδιαφόρως ἐσθίειν τὰ ἱερόθυτα ἐν πίστει
προσποιουμένους. 1 Kor 10,1–8 Τοὺς ἐκ τῆς παλαιᾶς τύπους καὶ τὰς ἐκεῖθεν σκιὰς
προεικονιζούσας τὴν μέλλουσαν ἀλήθειαν εἰς μέσον ἄγει ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος, ἵνα
σωφρονίσῃ τοὺς Korινθίους ἐκ τῆς τῶν παλαιῶν παραθέσεως. εἰ γάρ φησιν· οἱ εἰς
τὸν Μωϋσῆν βαπτισθέντες, ὃς ἦν τύπος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ καὶ τῇ θαλάσσῃ
καὶ φαγόντες τὸ μάννα, τὸ πνευματικὸν βρῶμα, καὶ πιόντες ἐκ τῆς πέτρας τὸ
πνευματικὸν πόμα κατεστρώθησαν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, εἰς μέθας καὶ πορνείας καὶ
εἰδωλολατρείας τραπέντες, ὅτι τὸν τύπον καὶ τὴν σκιὰν ὕβρισαν, τί οὐκ ἂν πάθοιεν
οἱ εἰς αὐτὴν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἁμαρτάνοντες; 1 Kor 10,9Ἐπειδὴ ἔλεγον· ἐμοὶ εἴδωλον
οὐκ ἔστιν· εὐχαριστῶ γὰρ καὶ ἐσθίω, τοῦτο, φησίν, ἐκπειράσαι ἐστίν. ὃ γὰρ μὴ
προσέταξενἸησοῦς ὅταν ὡς πιστεύων αὐτῷ ποιῇς, ἐκπειράζεις μᾶλλον ἢ πιστεύεις.
Τοῦτο φησι πρὸς τοὺς λέγοντας· ἐμοὶ οὐδὲν εἴδωλόν ἐστιν· εὐχαριστῶ γὰρ καὶ ἐσθίω,
ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἐκπειράζειν. ἃ γὰρ μὴ προσέταξεν ὁ κύριος ὅταν ὡς πιστεύων αὐτῷ ποιῇς,
ἐκπειράζεις μᾶλλον ἢ πιστεύεις. 1 Kor 10,11 Εἰς ὑμᾶς, φησί, κατήντησεν ἡ τοῦ
Χριστοῦ ἐπιδημία, μεθ' ἣν οὐκέτι ἔσται οὐκ ἐντολὴ οὐ νόμος οὐ προφῆται· τέλη γὰρ
λέγει οὐ τὴν ἐσχάτην γενεὰν καθ' ἣν συμπλήρωσις ἔσται τοῦ κόσμου, ἀλλὰ τὴν
τελευταίαν πολιτείαν τὴν ἐν Χριστῷ ἐφ' ᾗ τῶν αἰώνων ἡ συμπλήρωσις ἀπαντήσει. 1
Kor 10,13 Οὐκ ηὔξατο μὴ πειρασθῆναι, ἐπειδὴ ἀνὴρ ἀπείραστος ἀδόκιμος, ἀλλ'
οὕτως πειράζεσθαι ὡς φέρειν. Ἐκ τούτου δηλοῖ ὅτι ὑπέμεινάν τινας ἀηδίας ἐκ τῶν
πολιτῶν οἱ ἐν αὐτοῖς πιστεύσαντες. εἶτα οὐκ ηὔξατο αὐτοὺς μὴ πειρασθῆναι, ἐπειδὴ
ἀνὴρ ἀπείραστος ἀδόκιμος, ἀλλ' οὕτω πειρασθῆναι ὡς φέρειν. 259 1 Kor 10,14 Ὁρᾷς
ὅτι πάντα τὰ προειρημένα αὐτῷ τούτου ἕνεκα κατεσκευάζετο. Ἦλθεν ἐφ' ᾧ
κατεσκεύαζεν· πάντα γὰρ ὅσα προεῖπεν πρὸς τὸ ἀποστῆσαι αὐτοὺς τῆς
εἰδωλολατρείας ἐλέγετο καὶ κατεσκευάζετο. 1 Kor 10, Μὴ πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα αὐτῶν
ἀποβλέπετε οὐδὲν ὄντα, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὴν διάνοιαν καθ' ἣν θύουσι δαιμονίοις καὶ οὐ
θεῷ· τὸ γὰρ γινόμενον ὥσπερ εἰς ἄρνησιν γίνεται τοῦ θεοῦ. 1 Kor 10,22 Ἐπειδὴ
γέγραπται ὁ θεὸς λέγων διὰ Μωϋσέως αὐτοῖς· παρεζήλωσάν με ἐπ' οὐ θεοῖς,
παρώργισάν με ἐν τοῖς εἰδώλοις αὐτῶν, οἱ δὲ Korίνθιοι εἰδωλόθυτα ἤσθιον, διὰ
τοῦτό φησιν· ἢ παραζηλοῦμεν τὸν κύριον;–ἀντὶ τοῦ παροξύνομεν αὐτόν; –μὴ
ἰσχυρότεροι αὐτοῦ ἔσμεν; ἔδειξε διὰ τούτου, ὅτι οὐ θέλει ὁ κύριος εἰδωλόθυτα ἡμᾶς
ἐσθίειν. μὴ τοίνυν, φησί, θέλε ἃ μὴ θέλει ὁ κύριος, ὡς ἰσχυρότερος αὐτοῦ καὶ
συνετώτερος. Ἢ εἰς ζῆλον αὐτὸν κινοῦμεν καὶ παροξύνομεν; εἴρηται γὰρ παρὰ
Μωϋσεῖ· αὐτοὶ παρεζήλωσάν με ἐπ' οὐ θεοῖς, παρώργισάν με ἐν τοῖς εἰδώλοις αὐτῶν.
ταῦτα δέ φησιν, ἐπειδὴ εἰδωλόθυτα οἱ Korίνθιοι ἤσθιον. 1 Kor 10,25 Ἐπειδὴ εἰκὸς ἦν
αὐτοὺς ἀκριβολογουμένους μηκέτι τολμᾶν μήτε ὀψωνεῖν φόβῳ τοῦ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι
«εἰδωλόθυτον ἠγόρασας», παραμυθεῖται τὸν φόβον. συνείδησιν δὲ λέγει οὐ τὴν τοῦ
ἐγνωκότος ὅτι οὐδὲν εἴδωλον, ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ ἑωρακότος τὸν ἀγοράζοντα τὸ
english: Let him take part; for people do not join together with those in whom there is no agreement, but with those who join together in part. Since it also seems that the gospel does not use law, I have imitated its administration, so that I may participate in that which it intends to administer. Since it also seems that the gospel uses law, I have imitated its administration; for what that one said, this I administer.

He does not say this, that one of us all is preferred—for if people had not recognized themselves by looking toward the difficult thing—but making it clear that the image has been taken up by the nations toward the things said to him. All, he says, as if they are contending in this stadium of life: Jews according to law, Greeks according to error, but one is the word of the truth, the one winning and receiving the prize. Therefore run so that you are not left behind with the others.

What great thing, he says, if you exercise self-control over the flesh for the sake of the brother? Everything must be exercised by the one contending, from passion, from glory, and from all the rest; those indeed so that they might receive a perishable crown, but we an incorruptible one. He did not say this simply, but correcting those making it their business to philosophize for the sake of gluttony, supposing that the sacrificial food is not sacrificial food. He did not say this simply, but correcting those making it their business to eat the sacred things without distinction in faith.

The divinely inspired Paul brings the future truth into the midst by pre-figuring the types and the shadows from the old, so that he might bring the Corinthians to sobriety from the old tradition. For he says: those baptized into Moses, who was a type of Christ, in the cloud and in the sea, and having eaten the manna, the spiritual food, and having drunk from the rock the spiritual drink, were destroyed in the wilderness, turning toward outbursts, and fornication, and idolatry, because they insulted the type and the shadow; why then should not those sinning into the truth itself suffer? Since they were saying: 'To me, an idol is nothing; for I thank and I eat,' this, he says, is to test. For what he did not command...

By what you do, you are testing rather than believing. He says this to those saying, 'To me, there is no idol; for I thank God and eat.' This is to test. For whatever the Lord has not commanded, when you do it as one believing in Him, you are testing rather than believing.

He says that the arrival of Christ has reached you, with which there shall no longer be commandment, nor law, nor prophets; for he says they are ends, not the end of the last generation at which the fulfillment of the world shall be, but the final political order in Christ, upon which the fullness of the ages shall meet. Because of all these things, this one was being prepared. He came for the purpose for which he was being prepared; for all things which he spoke regarding turning them away from idolatry were being said and prepared.

From this it is evident that those who believed in Him endured a certain displeasure from the citizens. He says that they were to be tested in such a way as to endure. Do not look at the idols as if they existed, but look at the mind, through which they sacrifice to demons and not to God; for what is happening becomes as a denial of God. Since it was written that God said through Moses to them, 'You have made me jealous over not-gods, you have provoked me in their idols,' and the Corinthians were eating sacrificially to idols, he says: Do we provoke the Lord? Or are we stronger than He? He showed through this that the Lord does not want us to eat sacrificially to idols. Therefore, he says, do not want what the Lord does not want, as if you were stronger or more wise than He. Or do we move Him to zeal and provoke Him? For it is said by Moses: 'You have made me jealous over not-gods, you have provoked me in their idols.' He says these things because the Corinthians were eating sacrificially to idols.

Since it was likely that they were being precise and no longer dared even to buy food for fear of hearing, 'You bought idol-meat,' he consoles that fear. He speaks of a conscience, not the conscience of the one knowing that there is no idol, but the conscience of the one seeing the one buying...
